newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish govt eyes currency reserves to boost export.
newsitem.headline: Polish govt eyes currency reserves to boost export.

text.p: Polish Economy Minister Wieslaw Kaczmarek said he will ask the central bank to let some of its currency reserves be used to support exports under a package of pro-export measures approved by the government on Tuesday.
"I will ask the National Bank of Poland whether it is possible to use part of currency reserves to credit exports," Kaczmarek told a news conference, without going into details.

He said the package, due to go to parliament for approval, does not envisage requesting that the central bank devalue the zloty beyond the current level of one percent a month against a basket of foreign currencies.
"There is no agreement for such a solution as devaluation," he said.
The government should consider setting up an exports and imports bank that would help finance foreign trade, he said.
"An institution similar to an Exim bank should be created to support exports activity," he said. He provided no further details.
He said the adopted pro-export measures were needed to curb foreign trade deficit growth, which keeps accelerating with imports increase surpassing that of exports.

Last year, Poland had a $8.15 billion foreign trade gap and analysts say it could increase to more than $12 billion this year. In 1996, imports rose by more than 30 percent while exports expanded close to nine percent.
"The situation is not alarming...but we want to reverse tendencies we are observing," he said.

Kaczmarek said other measures included boosting export credit guarantees extended by the finance ministry's Exports Credit Insurance Corporation (KUKE). "Only 1.5 percent of Polish exports is supported by credit," he said.
He said the package also provided for quicker and simplified customs clearance procedures for reputable trading companies.
The government will also create an agency to promote Polish goods abroad, Kaczmarek said. He earlier said this institution was likely to incorporate the current Foreign Investment Agency (PAIZ).
He said the government would prepare a bill that would help curb what he called unfair competition by importers of cheap products.
"It is impossible that a pair of shoes has a declared customs value of six (U.S.) cents.... Preventive measures must be taken," he said.
